passage: Every night that week, Nkechi said the same thing in their shared kitchen in Leeds: "Tomorrow I'm starting the dissertation proposal. First thing." And every next evening Yara found her on the sofa, laptop closed, looking more tired than before. By Thursday Nkechi wasn't even saying tomorrow. She just stirred her noodles and said, "I'm hopeless." Yara thought about the pep talks she had tried, which hadn't helped. So instead she carried her own laptop to the table. "Twenty minutes. I'll do my reading, you do the easiest bit. Just the title page, maybe the reference list." Nkechi hesitated, then opened the file. Twenty minutes later she had a title, three references and half a sentence. She didn't stop at twenty. Yara pretended not to notice.

qa.q: What did Yara suggest Nkechi do in the twenty minutes?
qa.a: The easiest bit: just the title page, maybe the reference list.

qa.q: What does Nkechi's "I'm hopeless" suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: Each broken promise to start tomorrow has added shame, so she now sees herself as the problem, which makes starting feel even harder.

qa.q: Which choice of Yara's worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down beside Nkechi for a short, fixed time with the easiest piece; it swapped pressure for company and made the first step small enough to take.

qa.q: How does Yara see the week, and why does she stop giving pep talks?
qa.a: Yara watches her friend grow more tired and self-critical each evening, sees the pep talks aren't helping, and switches to quietly working beside her.

grounding: A flatmate notices a friend stuck in daily 'tomorrow' promises and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest part.

passage: In the hostel study room, Parveen had started noticing Ujjwal's pattern. At nine every night he would say, "Tomorrow I'll start the lab report, properly." By ten he'd be scrolling on his phone. In the morning he'd be quieter, skipping breakfast, muttering that he was the worst. On Monday the report was three weeks overdue and Ujjwal wouldn't meet anyone's eyes in the mess. Parveen didn't lecture; she had seen that make him shrink. Instead she pulled out the chair beside him. "I've got twenty minutes of problems to do. Sit with me? You just copy your data table in. That's the easy part." Ujjwal looked at the chair, then at her. Then he sat. The data table took twelve minutes. He kept going.

qa.q: What did Parveen suggest Ujjwal do first?
qa.a: Just copy the data table in, the easy part.

qa.q: How can you tell Ujjwal feels worse with each broken promise?
qa.a: He grows quieter, skips breakfast, calls himself the worst and won't meet anyone's eyes, which suggests growing shame.

qa.q: Why did Parveen choose to sit beside him rather than lecture?
qa.a: She had seen lectures make him shrink; a short shared session with an easy first task lowered the barrier without adding more shame.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ujjwal when Parveen pulled out the chair?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and wary at first, then relieved that someone offered company instead of judgement, which made sitting down possible.

grounding: A hostel friend sees a classmate repeatedly promise to start tomorrow and feel worse, and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest piece.

passage:
Dear Vijay,
I'm writing this instead of saying it, because saying it might feel like a lecture, and you've had enough of those. For three weeks I've heard you say, "Tomorrow I start revising for the backlog paper." And each time tomorrow comes and goes, you seem a bit smaller. Last Sunday you said you're just not made for this. I don't believe that. I think the paper has grown so big in your head that every start looks like a mountain. So here's my offer: Wednesday, 4 p.m., the second-floor reading room. Twenty minutes, both of us. You pick the easiest chapter, the one on definitions, and I'll do my own work next to you. If you want to leave after twenty, leave. No questions.
Your friend,
Preeti

qa.q: What does Preeti offer in the letter?
qa.a: Wednesday, 4 p.m., the second-floor reading room: twenty minutes together, starting with the easiest chapter, the one on definitions.

qa.q: Why does Preeti choose to write instead of speaking?
qa.a: Preeti worries that saying it aloud would feel like another lecture, and wants to offer help without adding to Vijay's shame.

qa.q: What makes Preeti's offer a workable first step?
qa.a: It is short, has a set time and place, begins with the easiest chapter and lets Vijay leave after twenty minutes, so starting feels small and safe.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel reading the line "I don't believe that"?
qa.a: Vijay may feel seen and a little relieved that a friend rejects the "not made for this" story, which could make the offer easier to accept.

grounding: A friend writes to a classmate caught in repeated 'tomorrow' promises and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest chapter.

passage: Twenty minutes and two cups of tea, that's what did it. I'm Manjula, and you asked on the student radio show what I did for my friend in second year. My classmate Shreya had a design portfolio due, and every night in the hostel mess she'd say, "Tomorrow I'm starting. Properly." The next evening, nothing, and she'd look a little smaller. By the third week she'd stopped coming to our Friday movie nights. I didn't lecture her. I just knocked on her door one Sunday with the tea and said, "Twenty minutes. Together. Only the easiest bit." She chose labelling her old sketches. Twenty minutes became an hour. She didn't finish that day, but she started. Now we have a Sunday tea rule.

qa.q: What did Shreya choose as the easiest bit?
qa.a: She chose labelling her old sketches.

qa.q: Why did Shreya seem to look a little smaller each evening?
qa.a: Each broken 'tomorrow' seemed to leave her more ashamed and doubtful of herself, so the promise meant to comfort her ended up making her feel worse.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Manjula's knock with tea and the offer of twenty minutes on the easiest bit; small and shared, it made starting feel possible instead of overwhelming.

qa.q: What was it like for Shreya to find Manjula at the door instead of a lecture?
qa.a: Probably a relief; Shreya was met with company and tea rather than judgement, which made saying yes much easier.

passage: I'm Zainab, and I share a bench with Rehana in our B.Com lectures. For a month I watched the same loop. Every Monday she'd say, "This week I start the tax assignment." Every Friday she'd say, "Monday, for sure." And each Friday she went quieter, rubbing her eyes, scrolling without really reading. I can't know exactly what was in her head, but it looked like each "tomorrow" was costing her something. Last Friday I said, "Stay after class. Twenty minutes, just you and me, and we only do the first question, the easy one." She hesitated, then nodded. We did the first question in twelve minutes. She laughed, surprised, and did the second too. On Monday she came in with three done.

qa.q: Which assignment did Rehana keep putting off?
qa.a: The tax assignment.

qa.q: What might Rehana have been feeling each Friday, and what suggests it?
qa.a: She seems increasingly discouraged: she goes quieter, rubs her eyes and scrolls without reading, as if each missed start weighed on her.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Zainab offered twenty minutes after class on only the easy first question; a small, shared start broke the loop, and that success led Rehana to keep going.

qa.q: What might those twelve minutes have been like for Rehana?
qa.a: Probably a surprise and a relief 🙂; a task that had loomed for a month turned out to be doable, which made the next question feel possible.
